h1: Setting a home beer fridge to the right temperature
title: Setting a home beer fridge temperature | Craft Beer School
desc: The right temperature for a home beer fridge, how to measure it properly, where beer belongs inside and when a second fridge makes sense.
teaser: Your fridge dial says 4. That number is almost certainly not degrees. Here is how to find out what your beer is really sitting at.
standfirst: Most home fridges are set for milk and leftovers, not beer. A cheap thermometer and ten minutes of adjusting tell you whether your beer is stored and served at the right temperature.
sections: Why the fridge matters more than the glass

Beer stales faster when warm. A pale lager kept at 30 °C, as it easily would be on an Indian kitchen shelf in May, can taste tired within weeks. The same beer held at 4 °C keeps its freshness far longer. Hoppy beers are even more sensitive. Their aroma fades quickly in heat.

So the fridge does two jobs: it keeps beer fresh while stored and it sets the temperature you pour at. Getting it right does more for the beer you drink at home than any glass or gadget.

• Storage for most beer: about 3 to 5 °C. Cold enough to slow staling, not so cold that anything freezes.
  • Serving pale lagers and light beers: about 3 to 7 °C, so straight from a 4 °C fridge is fine.
  • Serving pale ales, IPAs and wheat beers: about 6 to 10 °C. Take them out five to ten minutes before pouring.
  • Serving stouts and strong ales: about 10 to 14 °C. Take them out fifteen to twenty minutes ahead.

A single fridge at 4 °C covers everything. You adjust the serving temperature by giving warmer styles a few minutes on the counter. Our guide to beer serving temperature gives more detail by style.
Your dial is probably not in degrees

On many fridges with a mechanical dial, the numbers 1 to 7 are settings for cooling power, not temperatures. A higher number usually means colder. Digital fridges show a temperature, but the reading is for one sensor in one spot. The real temperature can differ by a few degrees elsewhere.

The only way to know is to measure. Put a cheap kitchen thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf and leave it overnight. Water changes temperature slowly, so it reads like a beer would, not like the air that swings each time the door opens. Read it first thing in the morning before anyone opens the door.

If the water reads above 5 °C, turn the dial one step colder and measure again the next morning. If it reads below 2 °C, or you find ice on anything near the back, turn it one step warmer. Make one change at a time and give the fridge a full day to settle, because it takes hours for the contents to catch up.

Check the reading again in the hottest months. A fridge in a 35 °C kitchen works harder than the same fridge in winter. The inside can drift warmer by a degree or two. Keeping the fridge out of direct sun and a few centimetres away from the wall helps it hold temperature.

The door is the warmest, least stable spot in any fridge. Every opening lets warm air in. The door shelves feel it first. Keep beer on a middle or lower shelf of the main compartment instead. Avoid the very back of the top shelf in some fridges, which can be cold enough to freeze a can.

Store bottles and cans upright. Bottle conditioned beers settle their yeast at the bottom rather than along the side. Less beer touches the cap. Keep beer away from strong smelling food like onions or open curries. Cans and sealed bottles are fairly well protected, but an open bottle picks up smells fast.

In many Indian cities, power cuts are part of summer. A closed fridge holds its temperature for a few hours. A full fridge holds it longer than an empty one, because the cold contents act as a store of cold. Keep the door shut during a cut and the beer will be fine.

Repeated warm and cold cycles are harder on beer than one steady temperature. If your area has long daily outages, keep your best beer at the back of a full fridge and drink it sooner rather than later. Voltage stabilisers protect the fridge's compressor. They do not change what happens to the beer.
When a second fridge makes sense

If you keep more than a dozen or so beers at a time, or drink a lot of stouts and strong ales, a small second fridge or a wine cooler can be worth it. Set it to 8 to 12 °C for ales and strong beers while the main fridge stays at 4 °C for lagers. A wine cooler is good for this because it is designed to hold a warmer, steadier temperature. Our guide on how to store beer at home covers longer storage.

Put a glass of water and a thermometer on the middle shelf before bed. Read it in the morning. If it is not between 3 and 5 °C, move the dial one step and check again tomorrow. Two mornings of measuring will tell you more than the dial ever has.
faqs: What temperature should a beer fridge be?
About 3 to 5 °C for storing most beer. Take ales and strong beers out a few minutes before serving to let them warm a little.
Is the fridge door a good place for beer?
Not really. It is the warmest and least stable spot in the fridge. Keep beer on a middle or lower shelf.
How do I check my fridge temperature accurately?
Leave a thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf overnight and read it before opening the door in the morning.
Yes. Upright storage keeps yeast at the bottom of bottle conditioned beers and limits contact with the cap.
